quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Kemal, would you like a cup of tea or coffee”?
quests.word: Kemal, would you like a cup of tea or coffee
quests.textToSpeak: Kemal, would you like a cup of tea or coffee
options: A /tʃ/ blend in “would you”, links in “like a” and “cup of”, and a strong “of”
A /dʒ/ blend in “would you”, elision in “like a”, and a strong “of” in “cup of”
Assimilation in “would you”, gemination in “like a”, and a weak “of” in “cup of”
A /dʒ/ blend in “would you”, links in “like a” and “cup of”, and a weak “of”
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend in “would you”, links in “like a” and “cup of”, and a weak “of”
quests.hint: Check the first junction for a blend, then see which later junctions join a consonant to a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Would you” has /d/ + /j/, which blend into /dʒ/. “Like a” and “cup of” each join a final consonant to a vowel, and “of” is weak, /əv/. Three different processes work together in one polite offer. A capstone listener separates them rather than hearing one blur.
quests.phoneticRule: A single polite offer can combine a /d/ + /j/ blend, consonant-to-vowel links and a weak function word.
quests.spokenForm: Kemal, wou-ja like-a cu-pəv tea or coffee

quests.instruction: Which junction in “Tomas, let’s meet at eight and get a good seat” is least likely to link a consonant onto a vowel?
quests.word: Tomas, let’s meet at eight and get a good seat
quests.textToSpeak: Tomas, let’s meet at eight and get a good seat
options: “meet at”, where a final /t/ meets a vowel and links onto it
“good seat”, where one consonant meets another consonant
“eight and”, where a final /t/ meets a vowel and links onto it
“get a”, where a final /t/ meets a vowel and links onto it
quests.correctAnswer: “good seat”, where one consonant meets another consonant
quests.hint: Look for the junction where there is no vowel to receive the consonant.
quests.explanation: Consonant-to-vowel linking needs a vowel at the start of the next word. “Meet at”, “eight and” and “get a” all have one, so each joins easily: “mee-tat”, “ei-tand”, “ge-ta”. “Good seat” has a consonant after /d/, so nothing can be carried over. Recognising a non-linking junction is part of hearing the pattern.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking carries a final consonant onto a following vowel, so a consonant-to-consonant junction does not link.
quests.spokenForm: Tomas, let’s mee-tat ei-tand ge-ta good seat

quests.instruction: Which two junctions in “Bilal, I’d like to hear about it over a cup of tea” include a linking /r/?
quests.word: Bilal, I’d like to hear about it over a cup of tea
quests.textToSpeak: Bilal, I’d like to hear about it over a cup of tea
options: “about it” and “cup of”
“hear about” and “over a”
“like to” and “hear about”
“it over” and “of tea”
quests.correctAnswer: “hear about” and “over a”
quests.hint: Spot the two spelled-r endings that sit directly before “about” and “a”.
quests.explanation: “Hear” and “over” are both spelled with a final “r”. In non-rhotic accents the /r/ is heard only when a vowel follows, and “about” and “a” provide one. “About it”, “cup of” and “it over” join other sounds instead. Linking /r/ depends on the spelling plus the next vowel.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking /r/ appears when a word spelled with final “r” is followed by a vowel in the next word.
quests.spokenForm: Bilal, I’d like to hear-r-about it ove-ra cup of tea

quests.instruction: In “Zane, I didn’t say she took it, I said he took it”, how is the second “he” likely said?
quests.word: Zane, I didn’t say she took it, I said he took it
quests.textToSpeak: Zane, I didn’t say she took it, I said he took it
options: Strong and stressed, /hiː/, to contrast with “she”
Weak, /i/, with a dropped /h/, as in ordinary speech
Weak, /hɪ/, with a short vowel and a clear /h/
Omitted, because it repeats information from earlier
quests.correctAnswer: Strong and stressed, /hiː/, to contrast with “she”
quests.hint: Ask what the speaker is correcting.
quests.explanation: A pronoun is normally weak, but it can carry contrastive stress. Here the speaker corrects “she” to “he”, so the second pronoun takes a strong /hiː/. The weak /i/ would hide the contrast. Emphasis changes the form even in a fast sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: A normally weak pronoun takes its strong form under contrastive stress, which signals a correction.
quests.spokenForm: Zane, I didn’t say she took it, I said HEE took it

quests.instruction: How might calm and annoyed deliveries of “Kasia, that was not what I asked for” differ?
quests.word: Kasia, that was not what I asked for
quests.textToSpeak: Kasia, that was not what I asked for
options: Calm: strong “was” and “what”; annoyed: weak “was” and “what”, with “not” dropped
Calm: a clear /t/ in “what”; annoyed: “what” dropped, with “not” unchanged
Calm: weak “was” and “what”, and a short “not”; annoyed: strong “was”, a long “NOT”, and a clear /t/
There is no difference, because stress does not change with emotion
quests.correctAnswer: Calm: weak “was” and “what”, and a short “not”; annoyed: strong “was”, a long “NOT”, and a clear /t/
quests.hint: Think about which words gain weight when a speaker is irritated.
quests.explanation: In calm speech the function words “was” and “what” are weak and “not” is short. In an annoyed delivery the speaker gives “was” and “not” more weight and may release the /t/ clearly. The grammar stays the same; the pattern of strength changes with attitude. A listener hears emotion partly through these shifts.
quests.phoneticRule: Attitude changes the balance of weak and strong forms, so emphasis and a clear /t/ mark an annoyed delivery.
quests.spokenForm: Kasia, thaʔ wəz noʔ wuh I asked for

quests.instruction: How can a listener tell “can” from “can’t” in “Dario, I can come, but I can’t stay long”?
quests.word: Dario, I can come, but I can’t stay long
quests.textToSpeak: Dario, I can come, but I can’t stay long
options: Both are /kən/, so only the next word shows the difference
“can” is weak, /kən/; “can’t” keeps a long vowel, /kɑːnt/, even if the /t/ is lost
“can” is long, /kɑːn/, and “can’t” is weak, /kən/
“can’t” is louder than “can”, and the vowels are identical in both words
quests.correctAnswer: “can” is weak, /kən/; “can’t” keeps a long vowel, /kɑːnt/, even if the /t/ is lost
quests.hint: Compare the vowel length in the two words.
quests.explanation: Positive “can” is usually weak, /kən/. “Can’t” is normally stressed, and it keeps a long vowel, /kɑːnt/, even when the final /t/ is lost. So vowel quality and length are better cues than the /t/ alone. This matters when meaning depends on a single small word.
quests.phoneticRule: “can” is reduced to /kən/, whereas “can’t” keeps a full, longer vowel, which is the more reliable cue than the final /t/.
quests.spokenForm: Dario, I kən come, but I CAAN’T stay long

quests.instruction: In a formal announcement, how is “Unfortunately I am unable to attend the meeting on Thursday afternoon” likely said?
quests.word: Unfortunately I am unable to attend the meeting on Thursday afternoon
quests.textToSpeak: Unfortunately I am unable to attend the meeting on Thursday afternoon
options: With full forms: “I am” is not contracted, and “to” and “the” are only lightly reduced
As “Unfortunately I’m unable tuh attend thuh meeting”, with every function word weakened as far as it will go
With “gonna” and “lemme”, which keep the tone relaxed and friendly
With every word stressed equally, which sounds natural even in formal speech
quests.correctAnswer: With full forms: “I am” is not contracted, and “to” and “the” are only lightly reduced
quests.hint: Think about what a formal speaker avoids even in a quick delivery.
quests.explanation: A formal style keeps “I am” in full and uses only light reduction of “to” and “the”. A casual style would contract it to “I’m” and reduce more. Informal items such as “gonna” and “lemme” would clash with the tone. Register shapes how much connected speech a speaker allows.
quests.phoneticRule: Formal register limits contractions and informal fusions, though light weak forms remain.
quests.spokenForm: Unfortunately I am unable tə attend thə meeting on Thursday afternoon

quests.instruction: Which pair of forms of “we should have asked and we would have known” fits casual speech?
quests.word: Marcus, we should have asked and we would have known
quests.textToSpeak: Marcus, we should have asked and we would have known
options: “we SHOULD HAVE asked and we WOULD HAVE known”, all strong
“we shouldn’t’ve asked and we wouldn’t’ve known”, with negatives added
“we should’s asked and we would’s known”, with “’s” in place of “have”
“we shouldəv asked and we’d’ve known”
quests.correctAnswer: “we shouldəv asked and we’d’ve known”
quests.hint: Choose the form that reduces “have” without changing the meaning.
quests.explanation: In casual speech “have” after a modal is weak, /əv/, and “would have” can become “would’ve” or “we’d’ve”. Strong forms would sound emphatic, negatives change the meaning, and “’s” is a different word. The casual form shortens without altering the sense.
quests.phoneticRule: Casual speech reduces “have” to /əv/ after modals and may contract “would have” to “’d’ve”, without altering the meaning.
quests.spokenForm: Marcus, we shouldəv asked and we’d’ve known

quests.instruction: Which form suits a polite service tone for “Mr Okafor, would you like me to hold the door”?
quests.word: Mr Okafor, would you like me to hold the door
quests.textToSpeak: Mr Okafor, would you like me to hold the door
options: A heavily reduced “d’ya wanna”, which suits a formal service tone
Fully separate words with no blends, which is typical of fast casual speech
A blend in “would you” and a clear “like me to”, which suits a polite tone
A dropped /h/ in “hold” and a slurred “the door”, which suits formal speech
quests.correctAnswer: A blend in “would you” and a clear “like me to”, which suits a polite tone
quests.hint: Pick the version that is smooth but still clear.
quests.explanation: A polite speaker may blend “would you” but keeps “like me to” clear enough to sound respectful. “D’ya wanna” is too informal for a formal address. Fully separate words sound stiff, not casual, and dropping /h/ in “hold” is not a usual pattern. Politeness shows in how much clarity is kept.
quests.phoneticRule: A polite service register allows light blending but keeps content words clear, avoiding heavy informal compression.
quests.spokenForm: Mr Okafor, wou-ja like me tə hold the door

quests.instruction: How would “Femi, put the green beans on the plate” most likely sound in fast speech?
quests.word: Femi, put the green beans on the plate
quests.textToSpeak: Femi, put the green beans on the plate
options: “puh the gren beans”: the /t/ is reduced and /n/ is unchanged
“put the greeng beans”: /n/ becomes [ŋ] before /b/
“puh the green peans”: the /b/ becomes /p/
“puh the greem beans”: the /t/ is reduced and /n/ becomes [m]
quests.correctAnswer: “puh the greem beans”: the /t/ is reduced and /n/ becomes [m]
quests.hint: Predict how the /n/ adapts to the lip sound that follows.
quests.explanation: The /t/ in “put” is often reduced before “the”. The /n/ in “green” sits before /b/, so it moves to the lips and becomes [m]: “greem beans”. A velar [ŋ] would suit a /k/ or /g/, not a /b/. Predicting the change from the next sound is the key skill.
quests.phoneticRule: A final /n/ before a bilabial /b/ is predicted to become [m], by place assimilation.
quests.spokenForm: Femi, puh the greem beans on the plate

quests.instruction: Where would place assimilation most likely occur in “Kwame, ten people came and sat beside Lola”?
quests.word: Kwame, ten people came and sat beside Lola
quests.textToSpeak: Kwame, ten people came and sat beside Lola
options: In “came and” (/m/ → [n]) and “beside Lola” (/d/ → [l])
In “ten people” (/n/ → [m]) and “sat beside” (/t/ → [p])
In “ten people” (/n/ → [ŋ]) and “sat beside” (/t/ → [k])
In “people came” (/l/ → [m]) and “and sat” (/d/ → [s])
quests.correctAnswer: In “ten people” (/n/ → [m]) and “sat beside” (/t/ → [p])
quests.hint: Look for an alveolar consonant right before a lip sound.
quests.explanation: The /n/ in “ten” comes before /p/, so it moves to the lips: [m]. The /t/ in “sat” comes before /b/, so it can become [p]. The other options have alveolars before alveolars, or reverse the direction. Place assimilation looks forward to the next sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar /n/ and /t/ commonly take the place of a following bilabial consonant.
quests.spokenForm: Kwame, tem people came and sap beside Lola

quests.instruction: Which change is most likely in “have to” in “Imani, we have to leave early”?
quests.word: Imani, we have to leave early
quests.textToSpeak: Imani, we have to leave early
options: /v/ becomes /f/ before /t/: “hafta”
/v/ becomes /b/ before /t/: “habta”
/t/ becomes /d/ after /v/: “havda”
/v/ is unchanged and “to” is strong: “hav too”
quests.correctAnswer: /v/ becomes /f/ before /t/: “hafta”
quests.hint: Think about whether /v/ can stay voiced before a voiceless sound.
quests.explanation: In “have to”, a voiced /v/ meets a voiceless /t/ and often becomes voiceless /f/: “hafta”. The result matches the following sound in voicing. A /b/ would change the manner, and a strong “to” would not be reduced. Voicing assimilation is predictable from the next sound.
quests.phoneticRule: A final voiced fricative may become voiceless before a voiceless consonant, as in “have to” → “hafta”.
quests.spokenForm: Imani, we haf-ta leave early

quests.instruction: Which words in “Delphine, the procedure for graduate education is gradual” contain /dʒ/ from /d/ + /j/?
quests.word: Delphine, the procedure for graduate education is gradual
quests.textToSpeak: Delphine, the procedure for graduate education is gradual
options: “graduate”, “education” and “gradual”, but not “procedure”
“procedure”, “graduate”, “education” and “gradual”
“education” only, because it is the longest word
“graduate” and “gradual” only, because they share a stem
quests.correctAnswer: “procedure”, “graduate”, “education” and “gradual”
quests.hint: Treat the same /d/ + /j/ pattern as one that also occurs inside words.
quests.explanation: In “procedure”, “graduate”, “education” and “gradual”, a /d/ is followed by a /j/ sound, and in normal speech they blend into /dʒ/. The pattern works inside words as well as between them. Recognising it in unfamiliar vocabulary is a transfer skill.
quests.phoneticRule: The /d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/ blend also operates inside words, so it transfers to new vocabulary.
quests.spokenForm: Delphine, the pro-see-jə for graj-uate ej-ucation is graj-ual

quests.instruction: Which two blends are likely in “Anselm, did you hear that Stuart is moving”?
quests.word: Anselm, did you hear that Stuart is moving
quests.textToSpeak: Anselm, did you hear that Stuart is moving
options: “did you” → /tʃ/, and “Stuart” → /dʒ/, with the voicing swapped
“hear that” → /ʃ/, and “Stuart” → /s/
“did you” → /dʒ/, and “Stuart” → /tʃ/ in some accents
“did you” → /ʒ/, and “moving” → /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “did you” → /dʒ/, and “Stuart” → /tʃ/ in some accents
quests.hint: Match each voiced or voiceless sound to its blended partner.
quests.explanation: “Did you” has voiced /d/ + /j/, so it becomes voiced /dʒ/. “Stuart” has voiceless /t/ + /j/, so in some accents it becomes /tʃ/. The voicing matches in each case. Swapping them would change the voicing, which does not happen.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiced /d/ + /j/ gives /dʒ/, and voiceless /t/ + /j/ gives /tʃ/, so voicing is preserved.
quests.spokenForm: Anselm, di-ja hear that Choo-art is moving

quests.instruction: Which junction in “Lucien, don’t cut your hair before the interview” follows the same /t/ + /j/ → /tʃ/ pattern as “meet you”?
quests.word: Lucien, don’t cut your hair before the interview
quests.textToSpeak: Lucien, don’t cut your hair before the interview
options: “don’t cut”, said as “don-chut”
“hair before”, said as “hair-rbefore”
“before the”, said as “befor-chuh”
“cut your”, said as “cut-chyer”
quests.correctAnswer: “cut your”, said as “cut-chyer”
quests.hint: Find the final /t/ followed by a “y” sound.
quests.explanation: “Cut your” has a final /t/ followed by /j/, so it can blend into /tʃ/. “Don’t cut” has no /j/, “hair before” offers a possible link, and “before the” ends in a vowel. The pattern depends on the sound that follows the /t/. Applying it to new words is a transfer test.
quests.phoneticRule: The /t/ + /j/ → /tʃ/ blend applies wherever a word-final /t/ meets a /j/, not only in set phrases.
quests.spokenForm: Lucien, don’t cut-chyer hair before the interview

quests.instruction: Which junctions are linked in “Folks, I’ll share my screen and walk you through it”?
quests.word: Folks, I’ll share my screen and walk you through it
quests.textToSpeak: Folks, I’ll share my screen and walk you through it
options: “share my” (an /r/ link) and “walk you” (a /tʃ/ blend)
“screen and” (a link) and “through it” (a /w/ glide)
“I’ll share” (a /j/ glide) and “my screen” (an /m/ link)
“walk you” (/k/ + /j/ → /tʃ/) and “screen and” (an /r/ link)
quests.correctAnswer: “screen and” (a link) and “through it” (a /w/ glide)
quests.hint: Look for a final consonant meeting a vowel, and a vowel meeting a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Screen and” joins a final /n/ to a vowel: “scree-nand”. “Through it” has a vowel meeting a vowel, so a /w/ glide appears. “Share my” and “walk you” do not behave as the other options suggest. Recognising which junction gives which link is the capstone skill.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant-to-vowel junctions link directly, and vowel-to-vowel junctions are bridged by a glide.
quests.spokenForm: Folks, I’ll share my scree-nand walk you through-wit

quests.instruction: Which delivery is the most natural for “Hang on, let me just check with Priya and get back to you”?
quests.word: Hang on, let me just check with Priya and get back to you
quests.textToSpeak: Hang on, let me just check with Priya and get back to you
options: All words equal and strong, with pauses between them, as in careful dictation
“Hang on, lemme jus’ check with Priya n’ ge’ back tə you”: reductions, with clear beats on check, Priya and back
“Hang on, lemme jus’ check wiv Priya n’ ge’ back tuh you”, with “th” replaced by /v/ as a rule
“Hang on, let me just check…” with every /t/ fully released and every vowel full
quests.correctAnswer: “Hang on, lemme jus’ check with Priya n’ ge’ back tə you”: reductions, with clear beats on check, Priya and back
quests.hint: Choose the version with reductions and clear beats on the key words.
quests.explanation: Natural speech says “lemme”, loses the /t/ in “just” and “get”, and weakens “and” and “to”, while keeping beats on “check”, “Priya” and “back”. Dictation-style delivery and replacing /ð/ with /v/ are not general patterns. A relaxed professional call blends reduction with clear stress.
quests.phoneticRule: A natural work call reduces function words and drops some /t/ sounds while holding beats on the content words.
quests.spokenForm: Hang on, lemme jus’ check with Priya n’ ge’ back tə you

quests.instruction: In “Everyone, we’re running a bit behind, so please bear with us”, which statement is most accurate?
quests.word: Everyone, we’re running a bit behind, so please bear with us
quests.textToSpeak: Everyone, we’re running a bit behind, so please bear with us
options: “running a” is said with a /k/ added, as “runnin-ka”, to separate the vowels
“bit behind” is said with the /t/ becoming /m/
“bear with” gains an intrusive /r/ before “with”
“running a” links /ŋ/ onto the vowel; “bit behind” often has a reduced /t/
quests.correctAnswer: “running a” links /ŋ/ onto the vowel; “bit behind” often has a reduced /t/
quests.hint: Check the sound at each boundary and what can plausibly happen there.
quests.explanation: “Running a” joins a final /ŋ/ onto the vowel, so it can sound like “runni-nga”. “Bit behind” puts a /t/ before /b/, which is often reduced. A /k/ is not added, a /t/ does not become /m/, and “with” does not gain an /r/. Each claim should fit the sounds involved.
quests.phoneticRule: A final /ŋ/ links onto a following vowel, and /t/ before /b/ is often reduced, whereas unmotivated sounds are not added.
quests.spokenForm: Everyone, we’re runni-nga bi’ behind, so please bear with us

quests.instruction: In the fast form “Mitch, can’ you ge’ the las’ ten pages sen’ over”, which sounds have been elided?
quests.word: Mitch, can’t you get the last ten pages sent over
quests.textToSpeak: Mitch, can’t you get the last ten pages sent over
options: The final /t/ in “can’t”, “get”, “last” and “sent”
The final /d/ in “can’t”, “get”, “last” and “sent”
The final /t/ in “can’t”, “get” and “last”, but not “sent”
The final /n/ in “ten” and “sent”, and the /t/ in “last”
quests.correctAnswer: The final /t/ in “can’t”, “get”, “last” and “sent”
quests.hint: List the last sound of each shortened word.
quests.explanation: “Can’t”, “get”, “last” and “sent” all end in /t/, and each is followed by a consonant or a weak word, so the /t/ is lost or reduced. The sounds are /t/, not /d/ or /n/. A listener who knows the pattern can restore the full words.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /t/ is often elided before a following consonant, and a listener can restore it from context.
quests.spokenForm: Mitch, can’ you ge’ the las’ ten pages sen’ over

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Emeka told me he would call, but he didn’t” in fast, casual speech?
quests.word: Emeka told me he would call, but he didn’t
quests.textToSpeak: Emeka told me he would call, but he didn’t
options: “Emeka toll me he’d call, but he didn’t”, with the /d/ of “told” becoming /l/
“Emeka told me he’d call, buh he didn’t”, with the /t/ of “but” released as /d/
“Emeka tol’ me he’d cal’, bu’ he didn’”
“Emeka told me he’d cal’, bu’ he didn’t”, with the /d/ of “told” fully released
quests.correctAnswer: “Emeka tol’ me he’d cal’, bu’ he didn’”
quests.hint: Choose the version in which the final stops are lost or reduced, and nothing new is added.
quests.explanation: In casual speech the final /d/ of “told” and the /t/ of “but” are often reduced or dropped, and “didn’t” loses its last /t/. The other options add a changed sound or keep the stops in the wrong places. Elision removes or reduces; it does not substitute new sounds.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision removes or reduces final stops in casual speech and does not replace them with different sounds.
quests.spokenForm: Emeka tol’ me he’d cal’, bu’ he didn’

quests.instruction: In “Soraya, the next train stops at the first platform”, which words most likely lose a /t/?
quests.word: Soraya, the next train stops at the first platform
quests.textToSpeak: Soraya, the next train stops at the first platform
options: “train” and “platform”, because each has a /t/ in the middle of a word
“stops” and “at”, because both are short function words
“at” only, because it is the only function word with a /t/
“next” and “first”, because each /t/ follows /s/ before a consonant
quests.correctAnswer: “next” and “first”, because each /t/ follows /s/ before a consonant
quests.hint: Spot where a /t/ is tucked between an /s/ and the start of the next word.
quests.explanation: “Next train” and “first platform” both have a /t/ at the end of a cluster, after /s/ and before a consonant, which is the classic elision position. The /t/ in “train” begins a stressed syllable, and “at” is more likely to link than vanish. Position decides.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /t/ after /s/ and before a consonant is the prime position for elision.
quests.spokenForm: Soraya, the nex’ train stops at the firs’ platform

quests.instruction: Which words carry the beats in “Picture this: I was standing in the rain with no keys”?
quests.word: Picture this: I was standing in the rain with no keys
quests.textToSpeak: Picture this: I was standing in the rain with no keys
options: “this”, “I”, “in” and “with”, because they come early in each phrase
Every word equally, because the story is dramatic
“was”, “the” and “no”, because they are short
“Picture”, “standing”, “rain” and “keys”, with small words squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: “Picture”, “standing”, “rain” and “keys”, with small words squeezed
quests.hint: Find the words that tell the story.
quests.explanation: The content words “picture”, “standing”, “rain” and “keys” carry the beats, and the small words between them are squeezed. A storyteller keeps this pattern even when the story is dramatic. Equal stress would flatten the story.
quests.phoneticRule: Storytelling keeps beats on content words and compresses the grammatical words between them.
quests.spokenForm: PICture this: I wəz STANDing in the RAIN with no KEYS

quests.instruction: In “Suddenly she turned round and said she had never seen it”, which items are most likely weak?
quests.word: Suddenly she turned round and said she had never seen it
quests.textToSpeak: Suddenly she turned round and said she had never seen it
options: “turned”, “round” and “seen”, because they are verbs
“Suddenly” and “never”, because they are adverbs
“she” (/ʃi/), “and” (/ən/) and “had” (/əd/)
None of them, because stories use only strong forms
quests.correctAnswer: “she” (/ʃi/), “and” (/ən/) and “had” (/əd/)
quests.hint: Pick out the grammar words, not the story words.
quests.explanation: “She”, “and” and “had” (an auxiliary) are function words and are normally weak. “Turned”, “round” and “seen” carry the action, and “suddenly” and the negative adverb carry the drama. A story still uses weak forms.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words are weak in narrative speech, and the verbs and adverbs that carry the story keep their stress.
quests.spokenForm: Suddenly shi turned round ən said shi həd never seen it

quests.instruction: How does a storyteller slow down for effect in “Lorcan, the door creaked open, and there, in the dark, was a figure”?
quests.word: Lorcan, the door creaked open, and there, in the dark, was a figure
quests.textToSpeak: Lorcan, the door creaked open, and there, in the dark, was a figure
options: By giving every small word a full vowel, so “and” becomes /ænd/ and “the” becomes /ðiː/
By dropping the consonants of every word so the voice sounds quieter
By lengthening stressed words and adding pauses, while keeping weak forms for the small words around them
By speaking faster on stressed words so they sound more urgent
quests.correctAnswer: By lengthening stressed words and adding pauses, while keeping weak forms for the small words around them
quests.hint: Think about which parts of speech can be stretched without changing how the small words are said.
quests.explanation: Slowing down is done with longer stressed syllables and pauses, such as “dark” and “figure”. The small words stay weak, so the rhythm still has contrast. Full vowels everywhere would make it sound stiff, and faster stressed words would reduce the effect.
quests.phoneticRule: Dramatic slowing uses longer stressed syllables and pauses, while the function words stay weak.
quests.spokenForm: Lorcan, the door creaked open, and ... there ... in the DARK ... was a FIGure

quests.instruction: Which statement about “law and order” in “Perrin, the law and order debate goes on” is accurate?
quests.word: Perrin, the law and order debate goes on
quests.textToSpeak: Perrin, the law and order debate goes on
options: In many non-rhotic accents it may be said as “law-r-and order”, with an intrusive /r/; rhotic accents usually do not insert it
In all accents it is said as “law-r-and order”, because “and” begins with a vowel
In rhotic accents it is said as “law-r-and order”, and non-rhotic accents drop it
The /r/ is spelled in “law”, so it is a linking /r/, not an intrusive one
quests.correctAnswer: In many non-rhotic accents it may be said as “law-r-and order”, with an intrusive /r/; rhotic accents usually do not insert it
quests.hint: Check whether “law” has an “r” in its spelling and which accents add one.
quests.explanation: “Law” has no “r”, so the /r/ before “and” is added, not linked. It occurs in many non-rhotic accents as a way of separating two vowels, and rhotic accents usually do not use it. It is optional and variable. Recognising it, without treating it as a rule, is the aim.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ is optional, appears mainly in non-rhotic accents, and is added where the spelling has no “r”.
quests.spokenForm: Perrin, the law-r-and order debate goes on

quests.instruction: Which feature of “Ottilie, the better butter is in a little bottle” depends most on accent?
quests.word: Ottilie, the better butter is in a little bottle
quests.textToSpeak: Ottilie, the better butter is in a little bottle
options: The /t/ in “better”, “butter” and “little”: a flap in General American, and a /t/ or glottal stop in many British accents
The /b/ in “better”, “butter” and “bottle”: a /p/ in General American
The vowel in “the”, which is /ðə/ in General American and /ðiː/ in British English
The /r/ in “better” and “butter”, which is dropped in both accents
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ in “better”, “butter” and “little”: a flap in General American, and a /t/ or glottal stop in many British accents
quests.hint: Look for a sound that changes by accent in the same position across the sentence.
quests.explanation: The /t/ between vowels, or before a weak syllable, is a flap in General American and may be a /t/ or glottal stop in many British accents. The /b/ does not change, the weak “the” does not behave as described, and “r” is kept in General American. This is accent variation, not error.
quests.phoneticRule: Intervocalic /t/ is the most accent-dependent sound: a flap in General American, and [t] or [ʔ] in many British accents.
quests.spokenForm: Ottilie, the beɾer buɾer is in a liɾle boɾle

quests.instruction: Which two accent-dependent features are likely in “Sunniva, the idea of better water was a good one”?
quests.word: Sunniva, the idea of better water was a good one
quests.textToSpeak: Sunniva, the idea of better water was a good one
options: A linking /r/ in “idea of” in all accents, and a flap in “good one”
A dropped /h/ in “idea of”, and a flap in “good one”
An intrusive /r/ in “better water” in rhotic accents only, and a /tʃ/ in “was a”
An intrusive /r/ in “idea of” (non-rhotic accents), and a flap or glottal stop in “better water” (by accent)
quests.correctAnswer: An intrusive /r/ in “idea of” (non-rhotic accents), and a flap or glottal stop in “better water” (by accent)
quests.hint: Pair each feature with the accent that produces it.
quests.explanation: “Idea of” can take an intrusive /r/ in many non-rhotic accents. “Better water” contains /t/ sounds that are flapped in General American or glottal in many British accents. The other options misplace the process or the accent. A capstone listener ties each feature to its accent.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ and flapped or glottal /t/ are tied to specific accents, so each feature should be matched to its source.
quests.spokenForm: Sunniva, the idea-r-of beɾer waɾer was a good one

quests.instruction: Which list of features fits “Dilys, could you tell her I’ll be there at eight”?
quests.word: Dilys, could you tell her I’ll be there at eight
quests.textToSpeak: Dilys, could you tell her I’ll be there at eight
options: A /tʃ/ blend, a dropped /h/ in “her”, a contraction, and an intrusive /r/ in “there at”
A /dʒ/ blend, a dropped /h/ in “her”, a contraction, and a linking /r/ in “there at”
A /dʒ/ blend, a clear /h/ in “her”, a contraction, and a /w/ glide in “there at”
A /dʒ/ blend, a dropped /h/ in “her”, gemination, and a linking /r/ in “at eight”
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend, a dropped /h/ in “her”, a contraction, and a linking /r/ in “there at”
quests.hint: Check each feature against its own junction.
quests.explanation: “Could you” has /d/ + /j/, so it blends into /dʒ/. “Her” is weak and loses its /h/, “I’ll” is a contraction, and “there at” has a spelled “r” before a vowel, so the /r/ is linking. Each of the other options changes one feature in a way that does not fit.
quests.phoneticRule: A final-stage listener maps each feature (blend, /h/ dropping, contraction, linking /r/) onto its correct junction.
quests.spokenForm: Dilys, cou-ja tell-er I’ll be there-rat eight

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “Perfect, I’ll see you at the station at half past six” is the most natural?
quests.word: Perfect, I’ll see you at the station at half past six
quests.textToSpeak: Perfect, I’ll see you at the station at half past six
options: “Perfect, I’ll see you at thə station at haf pas’ six”, with a weak “the”, a reduced “half” and a lost /t/
“Perfect, I’ll see you at the station at half past six”, with every word strong and separate
“Perfect, I’ll see yuh a’ the station a’ haff passt six”, with every /t/ dropped
“Perfect, I’ll see you at the stay-shun at half past-t six”, with an extra /t/ added
quests.correctAnswer: “Perfect, I’ll see you at thə station at haf pas’ six”, with a weak “the”, a reduced “half” and a lost /t/
quests.hint: Choose the version that reduces some words but keeps the message clear.
quests.explanation: A natural version has a weak “the”, a reduced “half” and a lost /t/ in “past six”. Strong separated words sound stiff, dropping every /t/ loses clarity, and adding an extra /t/ is not a connected-speech pattern. Reduction should be selective.
quests.phoneticRule: Natural speech reduces selectively: weak function words and a lost /t/ in a cluster, while the message stays clear.
quests.spokenForm: Perfect, I’ll see you at thə station at haf pas’ six

quests.instruction: Which two features are most likely in “Madison, what did you say she’d have done about it”?
quests.word: Madison, what did you say she’d have done about it
quests.textToSpeak: Madison, what did you say she’d have done about it
options: A /tʃ/ blend in “did you” and a strong “have” in “she’d have”
A dropped /h/ in “she’d” and a /dʒ/ blend in “say she’d”, said with a pause
A /dʒ/ blend in “did you” and a weak “have” (/əv/) in “she’d have”
A linking /r/ in “say she’d” and a strong “about”
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend in “did you” and a weak “have” (/əv/) in “she’d have”
quests.hint: Pick the two features that are common and that fit the sounds.
quests.explanation: “Did you” blends into /dʒ/, and “have” after “she’d” is weak, /əv/. The other options give the wrong blend, treat a pronoun as having /h/, add an /r/ with no spelled “r” in “say”, or keep “about” strong. The final check is to name only what the sounds support.
quests.phoneticRule: A final check names only the features the sounds support: a /dʒ/ blend and a weak auxiliary “have”.
quests.spokenForm: Madison, wot di-ja say she’d’ve done about it
